content:
In an effort to make the review process a bit easier, and to allow people to work more in a style which suits there needs, I was thinking about whether it is a good idea to introduce a distinction of an unmaintained and a maintained lean file in Physlib?

The idea would be:

  • maintained files are those which we commit to maintain forever, for which the review process is more rigorous, and which has to fit within the API style and theme of the project.
  • unmaintained files are those which we do not commit to maintain forever, if they break, we make a note of the commit at which they break and then just leave them (someone can come along later and fix them with an llm if need be). The review requirement for these will be 'is this mainstream physics, does it live in the right place within the repo, does it build right now'.

Naturally the property of being unmaintained should be one governed by dependencies. I.e. if a file is depends on an unmaintained file then it too should be unmaintained. Maybe think of a maintained file like a journal and a unmaintained file like the arXiv.

I'm going to pivot this idea a bit: Instead of unmaintained vs maintained files I think what I would like to try (even for a short trial period) is a new directory within the Physlib repo called ./PhyslibOL. The 'OL' here meaning 'one-look', referring to the type of review process for content in that directory. The idea being that

  • ./Physlib will continue to be kept to the same review standards it is now, and all files maintained forever (like a journal).
  • ./PhyslibOL will have a weaker review process (content is looked at once), with the balance that we don't promise to maintain it forever - if something breaks we just make a record of it.

In theory these could be two different repositories, but having them in the same repo makes it easier to deal with dependencies (and not having to worry about bumping another repo), and easier for people to find.

Like I said above, I think this is worth a shot as I think it solves some of the drawbacks of Physlib and similar projects that I've heard expressed.
will those be part of the build/CI check? or is the idea to have them in the repo but essentially text files that people "could" use but not really part of physlib?
I think the idea would be that they have to build/pass CI checks when first submitted. But we just don't promise to maintain them beyond that.
Hmm, what's the purpose of this? -- as in, what do you think is different about Physlib that makes it warrant this, while Mathlib/CSLib/etc. don't?

FWIW I have some informal system line this in FLT -- there are files which were written as experiments and aren't crucial to the key goal 1980s=>FLT and when they break, if I can't fix them immediately, I just add sorries. For example we have experimental definitions and calculations testing definitions.

Alex Meiburg said:

Hmm, what's the purpose of this? -- as in, what do you think is different about Physlib that makes it warrant this, while Mathlib/CSLib/etc. don't?

Yeah - this is a great question, and I understand that I have not articulated things the best here. I see a couple of problems with Physlib (and Mathlib and CSlib):

  1. It is not scalable. In a future where people can write Lean code easily with AI, the roadblock will be the review process. A slow review process is going to put people off submitting to these libraries. I think there is a real possibility that they get left behind.
  2. Academics typically want to work privately until they are ready to announce a result, for example alongside a paper submission. This sits awkwardly with Physlib's preference for small, incremental pull requests, and discourages contributions.
  3. People often have physics formalizations they would like to share, but do not want to take through the full review process required for the core library (at least imminently) - we have seen this a lot in physics.
  4. People may want to formalize a specific paper or experiment with a formalization idea, without restructuring it to fit the API structure of Physlib.

The idea of having a version of Mathlib that doesn't have such high standards of review does come up on this Zulip constantly. I think in Physlib we have more flexibility to try this. The idea is that ./PhyslibOL would sit hopefully at a nice intersection between 'allowing everything' and 'allowing only the best', so that it is still productive and useful, but is easier for people to submit to, and therefore easier to grow.

The idea would be the good code (including that which is used most often) in ./PhyslibOL, can be moved to ./Physlib - in this sense one could view ./PhyslibOL as a staging ground for ./Physlib. With this view I actually don't think this idea is 'unique', as I think the same concept is used in other open-source projects.

My gut reaction to this is also that I don't think it is a good idea. But I think if we want some say of what the future of formalization in this direction is going to look like, then I really think we need to think about how we adapt to the changing practices, and how we can best serve the wider community.

To give a bit more detail of what I envision it to look like:

  1. The project has a ./PhyslibOL top-level directory, in addition to a ./Physlib and ./QuantumInfo directory. (The reason I am not proposing a separate repo is to make dependencies easier).
  2. People can either choose to submit to ./PhyslibOL or ./Physlib or ./QuantumInfo.
  3. An automatic label is put on their PR accordingly.
  4. We the review PR according to where in the library it is.
  5. No matter what library the PR is in it has to pass CI and build, when the PR is made.
  6. When something breaks in ./PhyslibOL we don't fix it (we welcome other people fixing it with e.g. LLMs or something), but we will state it is not our responsibility.
  7. By 'we don't fix it', I mean we remove it from e.g. a PhyslibOL.lean file and make a note there about when it broke.
  8. If something in ./PhyslibOL is being used over and over again, we will aim to move it to ./Physlib (where we will put it under a more stringent review process).

I am expecting that LLMs will be pretty good at fixing the broken files eventually, which would prevent this from becoming a graveyard.

I think the way I have worded this, it may come across that the main feature of ./PhyslibOL is that it is unmaintained. To me the main feature is that it has a lower bar of review. (It is 'unmaintained' only because having a lower bar of review and putting a 'maintained' requirement on it puts a higher work-load on the maintainers of the project).

I personally don't see much harm in trying this, as it is something which we can easily revert if we decide we don't like it. If no one has strong objections to experimenting with this, I can set it up, and run this part of the repo, then after 2 months we can swing back here and discuss consequences, if we want to continue it etc.

I see. I agree that with the growing interest in largish AI PRs, this makes sense. (and indeed I think that some version of this could make sense for Mathlib too... I guess as a middle ground because Mathlib and sloplib, in the sense that it's still supposed to be useful for someone somewhere. And of course Mathlib doesn't permit any sorries.)
Okay, I'm on board, I think it's a good idea! :)

I'm not sure the "PhyslibOL" name is very explanatory -- unless you know specifically what it's standing for. you couldn't guess what it's about. Maybe something like "PhyslibExtras"? Or, similar to Mathlib, "PhyslibExtras"? (Other possible suffixes: "PhyslibLite" (because the review is light) or "PhyslibPlus" (because it's extra content on top)?)
I like PhyslibLite :).
Actually - am slightly worried that 'PhyslibLite' comes across as a light version of Physlib rather then light review. What about 'PhyslibAlpha'?
Added the basic infrastructure for this here: Physlib#1159. Happy to change name/anything else people want.
(Worth mentioning #general > Discussion for Lean Pool here which I just realized has a similar arxiv-like-idea behind it, though the implementation is different here).
I like PhyslibAlpha better than any of my suggestions. :)

Should we have a linter to make sure that nothing in Physlib or QuantumInfo imports stuff from PhyslibAlpha? (It would, probably, be pretty easy to enforce during manual review ... but I think a linter would be helpful)

Doesn't have to be a blocker on physlib#1159 but I think it would be good to have
I can try and cook something up now :).

Done - I did it a very conservative way which is just to use a python script to forbid lines that contain both import and PhyslibAlpha, since this deals with all import all ... as well as public import ... etc. One day a Lean script would be nice here :).
Yeah, I think that's the way to go, simple is fine. I hit approve. :)
I have set a Zulip reminder for myself to return to this in two-months, so we can see how it goes.

One thing I think we should do is make the policy and linters to say that results in PhyslibAlpha can depend on Tau Ceti results (although results in Physlib not)

Hi! I'm new here. I’ve been working on LeanCondensedMatter using Claude and GPT, where I have formalized the Bloch–De Dominicis theorem in condensed matter physics. The Linked Cluster Theorem is the next intermediate milestone. I’d like to discuss whether some of the more general and reusable parts of this development could be a good fit for Physlib.

Hi @naok1 , super glad to have you here :)

I am not familiar with condensed matter physics so will reserve my comments and wait for someone with a bit more expertise to guide you on the specifics. However, you might be able to get a feel for how to port some of your work by going through the condensed matter section of physlib. Currently its a bit underdeveloped which is why your help would be appreciated.
Furthermore, you could also go through other physlib sections like the classical oscillator as a guide for how physlib likes to develop different areas of physics.

Hi @naok1 ! Yes this would be a good fit, but the easiest way for us to tell for sure is by you opening a small PR with some of the stuff you think it might be good to include!

If it is AI generated just make sure it doesn't fall into some of the common pitfalls e.g. repeats stuff which is already in the project or Mathlib, documentation which is too verbose etc. And make sure you understand it :).

Thanks both! I’ll first go through the existing condensed matter section, as well as areas like the classical oscillator, to get a better sense of Physlib’s conventions and to check for overlap with existing Mathlib or Physlib code. After that, I’ll consider opening a small PR with a focused and reusable part of the development.
